h1: Beer with Parsi food from dhansak to patra ni machhi
title: Beer with Parsi Food and Dhansak | Craft Beer School
desc: Beer pairings for Parsi food: dhansak, patra ni machhi, sali boti, akuri and berry pulao, with the styles that suit sweet, sour and spicy.
teaser: Parsi food loves the sweet and sour balance. That makes it one of the friendliest cuisines in India for beer.
standfirst: Parsi cooking balances sweetness, sourness and spice in almost every dish. That balance gives beer a lot to work with. Here are the pairings we would reach for at a Parsi table.
sections: Sweet and sour is the Parsi signature

Parsi food grew from Persian roots and Gujarati kitchens, with a strong Bombay accent. Its defining trait is khatta mitha, the balance of sour and sweet. Vinegar, jaggery, tamarind and dried fruit turn up in dishes you would expect to be purely savoury.

That suits beer well. Malt brings its own gentle sweetness, while hops and carbonation provide the edge. The main thing to watch is that a beer's bitterness does not clash with the sugar in the dish. In general we keep bitterness moderate, between about 15 and 35 IBU, across a Parsi meal.

Dhansak is mutton or chicken cooked into a thick dal made from several lentils and vegetables such as pumpkin and brinjal. It is served with brown rice, which gets its colour from caramelised onions, plus kachumber and kebabs on the side. Sunday lunch, traditionally.

The dal is earthy, mildly sweet and warmly spiced. An amber ale or a Vienna lager is our first choice. The caramel and bread crust notes in the malt echo the browned onion in the rice. A best bitter at around 4% ABV works too, with enough hop character to keep the heavy lentils from feeling stodgy.
Patra ni machhi needs a light, herbal partner

Patra ni machhi is fish, usually pomfret, coated in a green chutney of coconut, coriander, green chilli and lemon, wrapped in banana leaf and steamed. It is fragrant, fresh and delicate.

Anything heavy will flatten it. A Kölsch or a German Pilsner is right: pale, crisp, with a light herbal or floral hop note that matches the coriander. A Belgian witbier, with coriander seed and orange peel in the recipe, is the playful match. Keep the beer cold (4 to 6 °C) and the glass small.
Sali boti and the meat dishes

Sali boti is mutton cooked in a tangy, slightly sweet tomato gravy and topped with sali, thin crisp potato straws. Salli par eedu puts eggs on the same crisp potato base.

For sali boti, think about the tomato and vinegar. A Märzen or a brown ale has enough malt sweetness to round off the acid, while the potato straws love carbonation. For the egg dishes and for akuri (spiced scrambled eggs) at breakfast, a hefeweizen is a lovely, gentle match if you are having a beer brunch.
Pickles, chutney and the wedding feast

A Parsi wedding meal, the lagan nu bhonu, is served on a banana leaf and often starts with sweet and sour pickle such as lagan nu achar, made with carrots and dried fruit in vinegar and jaggery. Then come fish, chicken farcha (spiced fried chicken) and mutton dishes before the pulao.

A long meal with this much sweetness needs a beer that refreshes rather than one that adds more sugar. A dry saison is our pick to carry through the whole banana leaf. Its high carbonation and peppery yeast character handle fried farcha and pickle alike, while its dry finish stops the meal feeling sticky. Saisons often sit at 5.5 to 7% ABV, so pour small and keep water on the table. If you prefer lager, a Helles does the same refreshing job at lower strength, though with less to say to the pickle.
Berry pulao and the festive plates

Berry pulao, an Irani cafe classic in Mumbai, layers spiced rice and meat with tart barberries. The fruit acidity and sweetness are the stars.

A Belgian dubbel, with dried fruit and caramel notes, picks up the berries, though its 6 to 7.5% ABV is best enjoyed in a small pour. For a lighter option, a fruity English pale ale does a similar job. To finish, lagan nu custard, the baked wedding custard, goes beautifully with a sweet stout or a milk stout, which brings chocolate and coffee against the caramelised top.
Serving notes for a Parsi table

Pour the lighter beers first, with the fish and eggs. Move to the amber and dark ones as the meal gets richer. Serve lagers at 4 to 7 °C, ales at 8 to 12 °C and stouts at 10 to 13 °C. Our guide to beer serving temperature explains why warmer is better for darker beers.

Try the dhansak with two beers, an amber and a Pilsner. One will make the dal taste sweeter, the other spicier. Working out which and why is the core of sensory training. For more on the general approach, see our Indian food and beer pairing guide.

Your first step: at your next Parsi meal, ask for a lager with the patra ni machhi and an amber beer with the dhansak, then swap them halfway. You will taste the difference straight away.
faqs: An amber ale, Vienna lager or best bitter. Their toasty malt echoes the caramelised onion brown rice. Moderate bitterness lifts the heavy lentils.
What beer suits patra ni machhi?
A Kölsch, German Pilsner or witbier. The fish is delicate and herbal, so it needs a light, crisp beer served cold.
Does beer work with sweet and sour dishes?
Yes, as long as bitterness stays moderate. Very bitter beers can taste harsh next to jaggery and vinegar, so keep to about 15 to 35 IBU.
